entries.04a1d6901e2705787dec46ed2daca7a3c15ffe71: <div sID="gen15119" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Eccl.11" sID="Eccl.11"/> <div eID="gen15119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15120" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15121" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A pressing exhortation to works of charity and bounty to the poor, as the best cure of the vanity which our worldly riches are subject to and the only way of making them turn to a substantial good account, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1-Eccl.11.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. A serious admonition to prepare for death and judgment, and to begin betimes, even in the days of our youth, to do so, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7-Eccl.11.10">ver. 7-10</reference>.
entries.6ffa7d155423653f03e37f21270d7947d3178abe: <div eID="gen15121" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15120" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Obligations to Be Liberal; Answers to Objections against Liberality.</title> <div sID="gen15122" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days. <hi type="super">2</hi> Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth. 3 If the clouds be full of rain, they empty <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> upon the earth: and if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be. <hi type="super">4</hi> He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap. <hi type="super">5</hi> As thou knowest not what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the way of the spirit, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> how the bones <hi type="italic">do grow</hi> in the womb of her that is with child: even so thou knowest not the works of God who maketh all. <hi type="super">6</hi> In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> alike good. <div eID="gen15122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15123" type="x-p"/> Solomon had often, in this book, pressed it upon rich people to take the comfort of their riches themselves; here he presses it upon them to do good to others with them and to abound in liberality to the poor, which will, another day, abound to their account. Observe, <div eID="gen15123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15124" type="x-p"/> I. How the duty itself is recommended to us, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">Cast thy bread upon the waters,</hi> thy <hi type="italic">bread-corn upon the low places</hi> (so some understand it), alluding to the husbandman, who <hi type="italic">goes forth, bearing precious seed,</hi> sparing bread-corn from his family for the seedness, knowing that without that he can have no harvest another year; thus the charitable man takes from his bread-corn for seed-corn, abridges himself to supply the poor, that he may <hi type="italic">sow beside all waters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.20">Isa. xxxii. 20</reference>), because as he sows so he must <hi type="italic">reap,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Gal. vi. 7</reference>. We read of the <hi type="italic">harvest of the river,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Isa. xxiii. 3</reference>. Waters, in scripture, are put for multitudes (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.5">Rev. xvi. 5</reference>), and there are multitudes of poor (we do not want objects of charity); waters are put also for mourners: the poor are men of sorrows. Thou must give <hi type="italic">bread,</hi> the necessary supports of life, not only give good words but <hi type="italic">good things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa. lviii. 7</reference>. It must be <hi type="italic">thy</hi> bread, that which is honestly got; it is no charity, but injury, to give that which is none of our own to give; first <hi type="italic">do justly,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">love mercy. "Thy bread,</hi> which thou didst design for thyself, let the poor have a share with thee, as they had with Job, <reference osisRef="Job.31.17">ch. xxxi. 17</reference>. Give freely to the poor, as that which is <hi type="italic">cast upon the waters.</hi> Send it a voyage, send it as a venture, as merchants that trade by sea. Trust it <hi type="italic">upon the waters;</hi> it shall not sink." <div eID="gen15124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15125" type="x-p"/> 2. "<hi type="italic">Give a portion to seven and also to eight,</hi> that is, be free and liberal in works of charity." (1.) "Give much if thou hast much to give, not a pittance, but <hi type="italic">a portion,</hi> not a bit or two, but a mess, a meal; give a large dole, not a paltry one; give <hi type="italic">good measure</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.38">Luke vi. 38</reference>); be generous in giving, as those were when, on festival days, they <hi type="italic">sent portions to those for whom nothing was prepared</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>), worthy portions." (2.) "Give to many, <hi type="italic">to seven, and also to eight;</hi> if thou meet with seven objects of charity, give to them all, and then, if thou meet with an eighth, give to that, and if with eight more, give to them all too. Excuse not thyself with the good thou hast done from the good thou hast further to do, but hold on, and mend. In hard times, when the number of the poor increases, let thy charity be proportionably enlarged." God is rich in mercy to all, to us, though unworthy; he <hi type="italic">gives liberally, and upbraids not</hi> with former gifts, and we must be merciful as our heavenly Father is. <div eID="gen15125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15126" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons with which it is pressed upon us. Consider, <div eID="gen15126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15127" type="x-p"/> 1. Our reward for well-doing is very certain. "Though thou <hi type="italic">cast it upon the waters,</hi> and it seem lost, thou thinkest thou hast given thy good word with it and art likely never to hear of it again, yet <hi type="italic">thou shalt find it after many days,</hi> as the husbandman finds his seed again in a plentiful harvest and the merchant his venture in a rich return. It is not lost, but well laid out, and well laid up; it brings in full interest in the present gifts of God's providence, and graces and comforts of his Spirit; and the principal is sure, laid up in heaven, for it is <hi type="italic">lent to the Lord.</hi>" Seneca, a heathen, could say, <hi type="italic">Nihil magis possidere me credam, quam bene donata—I possess nothing so completely as that which I have given away. Hochabeo quodcunque dedi; hæ sunt divitiæ certæ in quacunque sortis humanæ levitate—Whatever I have imparted I still possess; these riches remain with me through all the vicissitudes of life. "Thou shalt find it,</hi> perhaps not quickly, <hi type="italic">but after many days;</hi> the return may be slow, but it is sure and will be so much the more plentiful." Wheat, the most valuable grain, lies longest in the ground. Long voyages make the best returns. <div eID="gen15127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15128" type="x-p"/> 2. Our opportunity for well-doing is very uncertain: "<hi type="italic">Thou knowest not what evil may be upon the earth,</hi> which may deprive thee of thy estate, and put thee out of a capacity to do good, and therefore, while thou hast wherewithal, be liberal with it, improve the present season, as the husbandman in sowing his ground, before the frost comes." We have reason to expect <hi type="italic">evil upon the earth,</hi> for we are born to trouble; what the evil may be we <hi type="italic">know not,</hi> but that we may be ready for it, whatever it is, it is our wisdom, in the day of prosperity, to be in good, to be doing good. Many make use of this as an argument against giving to the poor, because they know not what hard times may come when they may want themselves; whereas we should therefore the rather be charitable, that, when <hi type="italic">evil days come,</hi> we may have the comfort of having done good while we were able; we would then hope to find mercy both with God and man, and therefore should now show mercy. If by charity we trust God with what we have, we put it into good hands against bad times. <div eID="gen15128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15129" type="x-p"/> III. How he obviates the objections which might be made against this duty and the excuses of the uncharitable. <div eID="gen15129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15130" type="x-p"/> 1. Some will say that what they have is their own and they have it for their own use, and will ask, Why should we <hi type="italic">cast</hi> it thus <hi type="italic">upon the waters?</hi> Why should <hi type="italic">I take my bread, and my flesh, and give it to I know not</hi> whom? So Nabal pleaded, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.11">1 Sam. xxv. 11</reference>. "Look up, man, and consider how soon thou wouldest be starved in a barren ground, <hi type="italic">if the clouds</hi> over thy head should plead thus, that they have their waters for themselves; but thou seest, when they are <hi type="italic">full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth,</hi> to make it fruitful, till they are wearied and spent with watering it, <reference osisRef="Job.37.11">Job xxxvii. 11</reference>. Are the heavens thus bountiful to the poor earth, that is so far below them, and wilt thou grudge thy bounty to thy poor brother, who is <hi type="italic">bone of thy bone?</hi> Or thus: some will say, Though we give but little to the poor, yet, thank God, we have as charitable a heart as any." Nay, says Solomon, <hi type="italic">if the clouds be full of rain, they will empty themselves;</hi> if there be charity in the heart, it will show itself, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 15, 16</reference>. He that <hi type="italic">draws out his soul to the hungry</hi> will reach forth his hand to them, as he has ability. <div eID="gen15130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15131" type="x-p"/> 2. Some will say that their sphere of usefulness is low and narrow; they cannot do the good that they see others can, who are in more public stations, and therefore they will sit still and do nothing. Nay, says he, <hi type="italic">in the place where the tree falls,</hi> or happens to be, <hi type="italic">there it shall be,</hi> for the benefit of those to whom it belongs; every man must labour to be a blessing to that place, whatever it is, where the providence of God casts him; wherever we are we may find good work to do if we have but hearts to do it. Or thus: some will say, "Many present themselves as objects of charity who are unworthy, and I do not know whom it is fit to give it to." "Trouble not thyself about that" (says Solomon); "give as discreetly as thou canst, and then be satisfied that, though the person should prove undeserving of thy charity, yet, if thou give it with an honest heart, thou shalt not lose thy reward; which way soever the charity is directed, <hi type="italic">north</hi> or <hi type="italic">south,</hi> thine shall be the benefit of it." This is commonly applied to death; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> let us do good, and, as good trees, <hi type="italic">bring forth the fruits of righteousness,</hi> because death will shortly come and cut us down, and we shall then be determined to an unchangeable state of happiness or misery according to what was done in the body. As the tree falls at death, so it is likely to lie to all eternity. <div eID="gen15131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15132" type="x-p"/> 3. Some will object the many discouragements they have met with in their charity. They have been reproached for it as proud and pharisaical; they have but little to give, and they shall be despised if they do not give as others do; they know not but their children may come to want it, and they had better lay it up for them; they have taxes to pay and purchases to make; they know not what use will be made of their charity, nor what construction will be put upon it; these, and a hundred such objections, he answers, in one word (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that observes the wind shall not sow,</hi> which signifies doing good; <hi type="italic">and he that regards the clouds shall not reap,</hi> which signifies getting good. If we stand thus magnifying every little difficulty and making the worst of it, starting objections and fancying hardship and danger where there is none, we shall never go on, much less go through with our work, nor make any thing of it. If the husbandman should decline, or leave off, sowing for the sake of every flying cloud, and reaping for the sake of every blast of wind, he would make but an ill account of his husbandry at the year's end. The duties of religion are as necessary as sowing and reaping, and will turn as much to our own advantage. The discouragements we meet with in these duties are but as winds and clouds, which will do us no harm, and which those that put on a little courage and resolution will despise and easily break through. Note, Those that will be deterred and driven off by small and seeming difficulties from great and real duties will never bring any thing to pass in religion, for there will always arise some wind, some cloud or other, at least in our imagination, to discourage us. Winds and clouds are in God's hands, are designed to try us, and our Christianity obliges us to endure hardness. <div eID="gen15132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15133" type="x-p"/> 4. Some will say, "We do not see in which way what we expend in charity should ever be made up to us; we do not find ourselves ever the richer; why should we depend upon the general promise of a blessing on the charitable, unless we saw which way to expect the operation of it?" To this he answers, "<hi type="italic">Thou knowest not the work of God,</hi> nor is it fit thou shouldst. Thou mayest be sure he will make good his word of promise, though he does not tell thee how, or which way, and though he works in a way by himself, according to the counsels of his unsearchable wisdom. He will work, and none shall hinder; but then he will work and none shall direct or prescribe to him. The blessing shall work insensibly but irresistibly. God's work shall certainly agree with his word, whether we see it or no." Our ignorance of the work of God he shows, in two instances:—(1.) We <hi type="italic">know not what is the way of the Spirit, of the wind</hi> (so some), we <hi type="italic">know not whence it comes, or whither it goes,</hi> or when it will turn; yet the seamen lie ready waiting for it, till it turns about in favour of them; so we must do our duty, in expectation of the time appointed for the blessing. Or it may be understood of the human soul; we know that God made us, and gave us these souls, but how they entered into these bodies, are united to them, animate them, and operate upon them, we know not; the soul is a mystery to itself, no marvel then that <hi type="italic">the work of God</hi> is so to us. (2.) We know not <hi type="italic">how the bones are fashioned in the womb of her that is with child.</hi> We cannot describe the manner either of the formation of the body or of its information with a soul; both, we know, are <hi type="italic">the work of God,</hi> and we acquiesce in his work, but cannot, in either, trace the process of the operation. We doubt not of the birth of the child that is conceived, though we know not how it is formed; nor need we doubt of the performance of the promise, though we perceive not how things work towards it. And we may well trust God to provide for us that which is convenient, without our anxious disquieting cares, and therein to recompense us for our charity, since it was without any knowledge or forecast of ours that our bodies were curiously wrought in secret and our souls found the way into them; and so the argument is the same, and urged to the same intent, with that of our Saviour (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Matt. vi. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">The life,</hi> the living soul that God has given us, <hi type="italic">is more than meat; the body,</hi> that God has made us, <hi type="italic">is more than raiment;</hi> let him therefore that has done the greater for us be cheerfully depended upon to do the less. <div eID="gen15133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15134" type="x-p"/> 5. Some say, "We have been charitable, have given a great deal to the poor, and never yet saw any return for it; many days are past, and we have not <hi type="italic">found it again,</hi>" to which he answers (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">v. 6</reference>), "Yet go on, proceed and persevere in well-doing; let slip no opportunity. <hi type="italic">In the morning sow thy seed</hi> upon the objects of charity that offer themselves early, <hi type="italic">and in the evening do not withhold thy hand,</hi> under pretence that thou art weary; as thou hast opportunity, be doing good, some way or other, all the day long, as the husbandman follows his seedness from morning till night. <hi type="italic">In the morning</hi> of youth lay out thyself to do good; give out of the little thou hast to begin the world with; <hi type="italic">and in the evening</hi> of old age yield not to the common temptation old people are in to be penurious; even then <hi type="italic">withhold not thy hand,</hi> and think not to excuse thyself from charitable works by purposing to make a charitable will, but do good to the last, <hi type="italic">for thou knowest not</hi> which work of charity and piety <hi type="italic">shall prosper,</hi> both as to others and as to thyself, <hi type="italic">this or that,</hi> but hast reason to hope that <hi type="italic">both shall be alike good. Be not weary of well-doing, for in due season,</hi> in God's time and that is the best time, <hi type="italic">you shall reap,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">Gal. vi. 9</reference>. This is applicable to spiritual charity, our pious endeavours for the good of the souls of others; let us continue them, for, though we have long laboured in vain, we may at length see the success of them. Let ministers, in the days of their seedness, sow both morning and evening; <hi type="italic">for who</hi> can tell <hi type="italic">which shall prosper?</hi>
entries.ec6e1ce1993568f00d77c3b66fabe82569779a31: <div eID="gen15134" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Caution to the Young; Exhortation to Early Piety.</title> <div sID="gen15135" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Truly the light <hi type="italic">is</hi> sweet, and a pleasant <hi type="italic">thing it is</hi> for the eyes to behold the sun: <hi type="super">8</hi> But if a man live many years, <hi type="italic">and</hi> rejoice in them all; yet let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many. All that cometh <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity. <hi type="super">9</hi> Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these <hi type="italic">things</hi> God will bring thee into judgment. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth <hi type="italic">are</hi> vanity. <div eID="gen15135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15136" type="x-p"/> Here is an admonition both to old people and to young people, to think of dying, and get ready for it. Having by many excellent precepts taught us how to live well, the preacher comes now, towards the close of his discourse, to teach us how to die well and to put us in mind of our latter end. <div eID="gen15136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15137" type="x-p"/> I. He applies himself to the aged, writes to them as fathers, to awaken them to think of death, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7-Eccl.11.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Here is, 1. A rational concession of the sweetness of life, which old people find by experience: <hi type="italic">Truly the light is sweet;</hi> the light of <hi type="italic">the sun</hi> is so; it is <hi type="italic">a pleasant thing for the eyes to behold</hi> it. Light was the first thing made in the formation of the great world, as the eye is one of the first in the formation of the body, the little world. It is pleasant to see the light; the heathen were so charmed with the pleasure of it that they worshipped the sun. It is pleasant by it to see other things, the many agreeable prospects this world gives us. The light of life is so. Light is put for life, <reference osisRef="Job.3.20">Job iii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.3.23">23</reference>. It cannot be denied that life is sweet. It is sweet to bad men because they have <hi type="italic">their portion in this life;</hi> it is sweet to good men because they have this life as the time of their preparation for a better life; it is sweet to all men; nature says it is so, and there is no disputing against it; nor can death be desired for its own sake, but dreaded, unless as a period to present evils or a passage to future good. Life is sweet, and therefore we have need to double a guard upon ourselves, lest we love it too well. 2. A caution to think of death, even in the midst of life, and of life when it is most sweet and we are most apt to forget death: <hi type="italic">If a man live many years, yet let him remember the days of darkness</hi> are coming. Here is, (1.) A summer's day supposed to be enjoyed—that life may continue long, even many years, and that, by the goodness of God, it may be made comfortable and a man may <hi type="italic">rejoice in them all.</hi> There are those that <hi type="italic">live many years</hi> in this world, escape many dangers, receive many mercies, and therefore are secure that they shall want no good, and that no evil shall befal them, that the pitcher which has come so often from the well safe and sound shall never come home broken. But who are those that <hi type="italic">live many years and rejoice in them all?</hi> Alas! none; we have but hours of joy for months of sorrow. However, some rejoice in their years, their many years, more than others; if these two things meet, a prosperous state and a cheerful spirit, these two indeed may do much towards enabling a man to <hi type="italic">rejoice in them all,</hi> and yet the most prosperous state has its alloys and the most cheerful spirit has its damps; jovial sinners have their melancholy qualms, and cheerful saints have their gracious sorrows; so that it is but a supposition, not a case in fact, that a man should <hi type="italic">live many years and rejoice in them all.</hi> But, (2.) Here is a winter's night proposed to be expected after this summer's day: <hi type="italic">Yet let</hi> this hearty old man <hi type="italic">remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many.</hi> Note, [1.] There are <hi type="italic">days of darkness</hi> coming, the days of our lying in the grave; there the body will lie in the dark; there the eyes see not, the sun shines not. The darkness of death is opposed to the light of life; the grave is a <hi type="italic">land of darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.21">Job x. 21</reference>. [2.] Those <hi type="italic">days of darkness</hi> will <hi type="italic">be many;</hi> the days of our lying under ground will be more than the days of our living above ground. They are many, but they are not infinite; many as they are, they will be numbered and finished when <hi type="italic">the heavens are no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.12">Job xiv. 12</reference>. As the longest day will have its night, so the longest night will have its morning. [3.] It is good for us often to remember those <hi type="italic">days of darkness,</hi> that we may not be lifted up with pride, nor lulled asleep in carnal security, nor even transported into indecencies by vain mirth. [4.] Notwithstanding the long continuance of life, and the many comforts of it, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> we must <hi type="italic">remember the days of darkness,</hi> because those will certainly come, and they will come with much the less terror if we have thought of them before. <div eID="gen15137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15138" type="x-p"/> II. He applies himself to the young, and writes to them as children, to awaken them to think of death (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9-Eccl.11.10">v. 9, 10</reference>); here we have, <div eID="gen15138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15139" type="x-p"/> 1. An ironical concession to the vanities and pleasures of youth: <hi type="italic">Rejoice, O young man! in thy youth.</hi> Some make this to be the counsel which the atheist and the epicure give to the young man, the poisonous suggestions against which Solomon, in the close of the verse, prescribes a powerful antidote. But it is more emphatic if we take it, as it is commonly understood, by way of irony, like that of Elijah to the priests of Baal (<hi type="italic">Cry aloud, for he is a god</hi>), or of Micaiah to Ahab (<hi type="italic">Go to Ramoth-Gilead, and prosper</hi>), or of Christ to his disciples, <hi type="italic">Sleep on now. "Rejoice, O young man! in thy youth,</hi> live a merry life, follow thy sports, and take thy pleasures; <hi type="italic">let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth,</hi> cheer thee with its fancies and foolish hopes; entertain thyself with thy pleasing dreams; <hi type="italic">walk in the ways of thy heart;</hi> do whatever thou hast a mind to do, and stick at nothing that may gratify the sensual appetite. <hi type="italic">Quicquid libet, licet</hi>—<hi type="italic">Make thy will thy law. Walk in the ways of thy heart, and</hi> let thy heart walk after <hi type="italic">thy eyes,</hi> a rambling heart after a roving eye; what is pleasing in thy own eyes do it, whether it be pleasing in the eyes of God or no." Solomon speaks thus ironically to the young man to intimate, (1.) That this is that which he would do, and which he would fain have leave to do, in which he places his happiness and on which he sets his heart. (2.) That he wishes all about him would give him this counsel, would prophesy to him such smooth things as these, and cannot brook any advice to the contrary, but reckons those his enemies that bid him be sober and serious. (3.) To expose his folly, and the great absurdity of a voluptuous vicious course of life. The very description of it, if men would see things entirely, and judge of them impartially, is enough to show how contrary to reason those act that live such a life. The very opening of the cause is enough to determine it, without any argument. (4.) To show that if men give themselves to such a course of life as this it is just with God to give them up to it, to abandon them to their own heart's lusts, that they may <hi type="italic">walk in their own counsels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.4.7">Hos. iv. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen15139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15140" type="x-p"/> 2. A powerful check given to these vanities and pleasures: "<hi type="italic">Know thou that for all these things God shall bring thee into judgment,</hi> and duly consider that, and then live such a luxurious life if thou canst, if thou darest." This is a <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kolasterion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a corrective</hi> to the foregoing concession, and plucks in the reins he had laid on the neck of the young man's lust. "<hi type="italic">Know then,</hi> for a certainty, that, if thou dost take such a liberty as this, it will be thy everlasting ruin; thou hast to do with a God who will not let it go unpunished." Note, (1.) There is a judgment to come. (2.) We must every one of us be brought into judgment, however we may now put far from us that evil day. (3.) We shall be reckoned with for all our carnal mirth and sensual pleasures in that day. (4.) It is good for all, but especially for young people, to know and consider this, that they may not, by the indulgence of their youthful lusts, <hi type="italic">treasure up unto themselves wrath against that day of wrath,</hi> the wrath of the Lamb. <div eID="gen15140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15141" type="x-p"/> 3. A word of caution and exhortation inferred from all this, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.10">v. 10</reference>. Let young people look to themselves and manage well both their souls and their bodies, their heart and their flesh. (1.) Let them take care that their minds be not lifted up with pride, nor disturbed with anger, or any sinful passion: <hi type="italic">Remove sorrow,</hi> or anger, <hi type="italic">from thy heart;</hi> the word signifies any disorder or perturbation of the mind. Young people are apt to be impatient of check and control, to vex and fret at any thing that is humbling and mortifying to them, and their proud hearts rise against every thing that crosses and contradicts them. They are so set upon that which is pleasing to sense that they cannot bear any thing that is displeasing, but it goes with sorrow to their heart. Their pride often disquiets them, and makes them uneasy. "Put that away, and the love of the world, and lay thy expectations low from the creature, and then disappointments will not be occasions of sorrow and anger to thee." Some by sorrow here understand that carnal mirth described <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">v. 9</reference>, the end of which will be bitterness and sorrow. Let them keep at a distance from every thing which will be sorrow in the reflection. (2.) Let them take care that their bodies be not defiled by intemperance, uncleanness, or any fleshly lusts: "<hi type="italic">Put away evil from the flesh,</hi> and let not the members of thy body be instruments of unrighteousness. The evil of sin will be the evil of punishment, and that which thou art fond of, as good for the flesh, because it gratifies the appetites of it, will prove evil, and hurtful to it, and therefore put it far from thee, the further the better." <div eID="gen15141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15142" type="x-p"/> III. The preacher, to enforce his admonition both to old and young, urges, as an effectual argument, that which is the great argument of his discourse, the vanity of all present things, their uncertainty and insufficiency. 1. He reminds old people of this (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that comes is vanity;</hi> yea, though <hi type="italic">a man live many years and rejoice in them all,</hi> All that has come already, and all that is yet to come, how much soever men promise themselves from the concluding scenes, it is all <hi type="italic">vanity.</hi> What will be will do no more to make men happy than what has been. <hi type="italic">All that come</hi> into the world are <hi type="italic">vanity;</hi> they are altogether so, at their best estate. 2. He reminds young people of this: <hi type="italic">Childhood and youth are vanity.</hi> The dispositions and actions of childhood and youth have in them a great deal of impertinence and iniquity, sinful vanity, which young people have need to watch against and get cured. The pleasures and advantages of childhood and youth have in them no certainty, satisfaction, nor continuance. They are passing away; these flowers will soon wither, and these blossoms fall; let them therefore be knit into good fruit, which will continue and abound to a good account.  <chapter eID="Eccl.11"/> <div eID="gen15142" type="x-p"/>

entries.5fc43e4d327602b419c119f29a82dff56b7eaddc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8169"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen12753" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1-Eccl.11.10">Ec 11:1-10</reference>.<div eID="gen12753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8169"/>1. <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference> shows that charity is here inculcated.<div eID="gen12754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bread--</hi>bread corn. As in the Lord's prayer, all things needful for the body and soul. Solomon reverts to the sentiment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waters--</hi>image from the custom of sowing seed by casting it from boats into the overflowing waters of the Nile, or in any marshy ground. When the waters receded, the grain in the alluvial soil sprang up (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.20">Is 32:20</reference>). "Waters" express multitudes, so <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Re 17:15</reference>; also the seemingly hopeless character of the recipients of the charity; but it shall prove at last to have been not thrown away (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>). <div eID="gen12756" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c86f31e1628c58dd3d4dc26446a42aa08d4d528: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8170"/><div sID="gen12757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8170"/><hi type="bold">2. portion--</hi>of thy bread.<div eID="gen12757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven--</hi>the perfect number.<div eID="gen12758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eight--</hi>even to more than seven; that is, "to many" (so "waters," <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Ec 11:1</reference>), nay, even to very many in need (<reference osisRef="Job.5.19">Job 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mi 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil--</hi>The day may be near, when you will need the help of those whom you have bound to you by kindnesses (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.9">Lu 16:9</reference>). The very argument which covetous men use against liberality (namely, that bad times may come), the wise man uses for it. <div eID="gen12760" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a599812386e1312b79cce136982890980eeaeb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8171"/><div sID="gen12761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8171"/><hi type="bold">3. clouds--</hi>answering to "evil" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference>), meaning, When the times of evil are fully ripe, evil must come; and speculations about it beforehand, so as to prevent one sowing seed of liberality, are vain (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Ec 11:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tree--</hi>Once the storm uproots it, it lies either northward or southward, according as it fell. So man's character is unchangeable, whether for hell or heaven, once that death overtakes him (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Re 22:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">14, 15</reference>). Now is his time for liberality, before the evil days come (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Ec 12:1</reference>). <div eID="gen12762" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5b85aecda8f5397c7906e5f7fba6282b8c685c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8172"/><div sID="gen12763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8172"/>4. Therefore sow thy charity in faith, without hesitancy or speculation as to results, because they may not seem promising (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>). So in <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Ec 11:1</reference>, man is told to "cast his bread corn" on the seemingly unpromising "waters" (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.5">Psa 126:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.6">6</reference>). The farmer would get on badly, who, instead of sowing and reaping, spent his time in watching the wind and clouds. <div eID="gen12763" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a3b101dd712dc68ff38e47c915f9999f2e98cc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8173"/><div sID="gen12764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8173"/><hi type="bold">5. spirit--</hi>How the soul animates the body! Thus the transition to the formation of the body "in the womb" is more natural, than if with Maurer we translate it "wind" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ec 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.8">Joh 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen12764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bones ... grow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.10.8">Job 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen12765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowest not the works of God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">9:12</reference>). <div eID="gen12766" type="x-p"/>
entries.210d682d8fbe7d7ffa0e6e212897ecf50a7e2ec4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8174"/><div sID="gen12767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8174"/><hi type="bold">6. morning ... evening--</hi>early and late; when young and when old; in sunshine and under clouds.<div eID="gen12767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seed--</hi>of godly works (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">Ho 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">2Co 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>).<div eID="gen12768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prosper--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.55.10">Is 55:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen12769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">both ... alike--</hi>Both the unpromising and the promising sowing may bear good fruit in others; certainly they shall to the faithful sower. <div eID="gen12770" type="x-p"/>
entries.3857be308d72fd145bec1b9a2b4a6d4f21d1a030: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8175"/><div sID="gen12771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8175"/><hi type="bold">7. light--</hi>of life (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Ec 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.19">Psa 49:19</reference>). Life is enjoyable, especially to the godly. <div eID="gen12771" type="x-p"/>
entries.543fb78f671b76e743cd509feb890445335d5d5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8176"/><div sID="gen12772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8176"/>8. But while man thankfully enjoys life, "let him remember" it will not last for ever. The "many days of darkness," that is, the unseen world (<reference osisRef="Job.10.21">Job 10:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.12">Psa 88:12</reference>), also days of "evil" in this world (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference>), are coming; therefore sow the good seed while life and good days last, which are not too long for accomplishing life's duties.<div eID="gen12772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">All that cometh--</hi>that is, All that followeth in the evil and dark days is vain, as far as work for God is concerned (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>). <div eID="gen12773" type="x-p"/>
entries.362e966936f5cfd209b58b3a5ae6e28d591d45f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8177"/><div sID="gen12774" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8177"/><hi type="bold">9. Rejoice--</hi>not advice, but warning. So <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.15">1Ki 22:15</reference>, is irony; if thou dost rejoice (carnally, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.2">Ec 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">7:2</reference>, not moderately, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">Ec 5:18</reference>), &c., then "know that ... God will bring thee into judgment" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">12:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">youth ... youth--</hi>distinct Hebrew words, adolescence or boyhood (before <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.10">Ec 11:10</reference>), and full-grown youth. It marks the gradual progress in self-indulgence, to which the young especially are prone; they see the roses, but do not discover the thorns, until pierced by them. Religion will cost self-denial, but the want of it infinitely more (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.28">Lu 14:28</reference>). <div eID="gen12775" type="x-p"/>
entries.4713b498f51931e97d2a450991cfa0331bdcc35b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8178"/><div sID="gen12776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8178"/><hi type="bold">10. sorrow--</hi>that is, the lusts that end in "sorrow," opposed to "rejoice," and "heart cheer thee" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>), Margin, "anger," that is, all "ways of thine heart"; "remove," &c., is thus opposed to "walk in," &c. (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>the bodily organ by which the sensual thoughts of the "heart" are embodied in acts.<div eID="gen12777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">childhood--</hi>rather, "boyhood"; the same Hebrew word as the first, "youth" in <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>. A motive for self-restraint; the time is coming when the vigor of youth on which thou reliest, will seem vain, except in so far as it has been given to God (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Ec 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen12778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">youth--</hi>literally, the dawn of thy days. <chapter eID="Eccl.11"/>

entries.b9ceee47754d3c01fd00c99ba3869c13600b8bc1: <div eID="gen25711" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25712" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25713" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25713" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25712" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25714" type="x-p"/> Give alms to all, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.1-Ecc.11.4">Ecc 11:1-4</reference>. The works of God unknown to man, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference>. Diligence necessary, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.6">Ecc 11:6</reference>. Prosperity frequently succeeded by adversity, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.7">Ecc 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.8">Ecc 11:8</reference>. There will be a day of judgment, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.9">Ecc 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.10">Ecc 11:10</reference>. <div eID="gen25714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25716" type="x-p"/> Cast thy bread upon the waters - An allusion to the sowing of rice; which was sown upon muddy ground, or ground covered with water, and trodden in by the feet of cattle: it thus took root, and grew, and was found after many days in a plentiful harvest. Give alms to the poor, and it will be as seed sown in good ground. God will cause thee afterwards to receive it with abundant increase. The Targum understands it of giving bread to poor sailors. The Vulgate and my old Bible have the same idea. Send thi brede upon men passing waters.
entries.a522a375cba753d6af7024dae540283f4ff6518b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25717" type="x-p"/> Give a portion to seven - Never cease giving while thou seest a person in distress, and hast wherewithal to relieve him. <div eID="gen25717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25718" type="x-p"/> Thou knowest not what evil - Such may be the change of times, that thou mayest yet stand in need of similar help thyself. Do as thou wouldst be done by.
entries.5b11d3fea46a453e45f016c9b2519e9670150dba: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25719" type="x-p"/> If the clouds be full of rain - Act as the clouds; when they are full they pour out their water indifferently on the field and on the desert. By giving charity indiscriminately, it may be that thou wilt often give it to the unworthy: but thou shouldst ever consider that he is an object of thy charity, who appears to be in real want; and better relieve or give to a hundred worthless persons, than pass by one who is in real distress. <div eID="gen25719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25720" type="x-p"/> Where the tree falleth, there it shall be - Death is at no great distance; thou hast but a short time to do good. Acquire a heavenly disposition while here; for there will be no change after this life. If thou die in the love of God, and in the love of man, in that state wilt thou be found in the day of judgment. If a tree about to fall lean to the north, to the north it will fall; if to the south, it will fall to that quarter. In whatever disposition or state of soul thou diest, in that thou wilt be found in the eternal world. Death refines nothing, purifies nothing, kills no sin, helps to no glory. Let thy continual bent and inclination be to God, to holiness, to charity, to mercy, and to heaven: then, fall when thou mayest, thou wilt fall well.
entries.c13c05fbb4fd6db963f3dcf149b1b3e1212c9268: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25721" type="x-p"/> He that observeth the wind shall not sow! - The man that is too scrupulous is never likely to succeed in any thing. If a man neither plough nor sow till the weather is entirely to his mind, the season will in all probability pass before he will have done any thing: so, if thou be too nice in endeavoring to find out who are the impostors among those who profess to be in want, the real object may perish, whom otherwise thou mightest have relieved, and whose life might have been thereby saved. Those very punctilious and scrupulous people, who will sift every thing to the bottom in every case, and, before they will act, must be fully satisfied on all points, seldom do any good, and are themselves generally good for nothing. While they are observing the clouds and the rain, others have joined hands with God, and made a poor man live.
entries.32203a02170abf90a5903968d0354231f4044b68: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25722" type="x-p"/> As thou knowest not - the way of the spirit - Why God should have permitted such an such persons to fall into want, and how they came into all their distresses, thou canst not tell, no more than thou canst how their soul is united to their body, how it came to inform that body, or how the child was formed in the womb of its mother. Nor canst thou discern the end which God has in view in these things. He maketh all, every thing is open to him; and take heed lest, while pretending motives of scrupulosity and prudence, in not relieving the distresses of those thou pretendest to suspect to be unworthy, he does not see that a love of money is the motive of thy conduct, and a want of the bowels of mercy the cause why thou drivest this suspected beggar from thy door.
entries.4b90bf2423d99da69d28c830ceb518e452826188: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25723" type="x-p"/> In the morning sow thy seed - Be ready at all times to show mercy; begin in the morning, continue till the evening. Thou knowest not the most worthy object; it is enough that God knoweth; and if thy motive be good, he will applaud and reward thee; not according to the worthiness or unworthiness of the object of thy charity, but according to the motive which induced thee to relieve him.
entries.502277e55bb764370d4546bd16036046b6a69fc8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25724" type="x-p"/> Truly the light is sweet - Life is dear to every man as the light of the sun is to the eye. A man would give all that he has for his life, and it is particularly dear to him when he is in ease and affluence: but let each remember that,
entries.4ab5ce7d11340262e8befd42f2d6c46f7187f232: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25725" type="x-p"/> If a man live many years - And even have prosperity through the whole; yet the days of darkness - times of affliction, weakness, and perhaps old age, will be many. If he die not a violent death, which no man can wish, he will die a lingering death; and this is ordinarily attended with many pains, and many sorrows; therefore let him prepare to meet his God; and to carry this thought through life, that all must terminate in death. The writer of Ecclesiasticus, 7:36, has a good saying, similar to this: "Whatsoever thou takest in hand, remember thy End; and thou shalt never do amiss;" ουκ ἁμαρτησεις, thou wilt not sin.
entries.784a57b349c1817f98c5b54d52ac76b6e027e481: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25726" type="x-p"/> Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth - Youth is devoid of cares; and, consequently, of many perplexities and distresses. Were it not so, we should have no old men; nay, perhaps not one even of middle ape. It is in the order of a most gracious God, that the young should rejoice in their youth; but they should make such a moderate use of all their enjoyments, that they may not be confounded in the day of judgment. But, O young man, if thou wilt follow the propensities of thy own heart, the noisy mirth of the fool, and the dissipation of the profligate - go on; take thy full swing; but take this with thee, that "for all these things, God will judge thee;" and if the righteous are scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?
entries.3b5172eb22f04505bf86c5e31d3cbd26785b5cab: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25727" type="x-p"/> Therefore remove sorrow - כעס caas, anger; every kind of violent passion, all filthiness of the flesh and spirit. "Childhood and youth are vanity;" they pass away and come to nothing. Eternity alone is permanent; live for eternity.  <chapter eID="Eccl.11"/> <div eID="gen25727" type="x-p"/>

entries.acb88de5a7d04dd68a3d35f2d220eda180f85ace: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Ecc 11:1</reference> “Let thy bread go forth over the watery mirror: for in the course of many days shalt thou find it.” Most interpreters, chiefly the Talm., Midrash, and Targ.,<note placement="foot">The Midrash tells the following story: Rabbi Akiba sees a ship wrecked which carried in it one learned in the law. He finds him again actively engaged in Cappadocia. What whale, he asked him, has vomited thee out upon dry land? How hast thou merited this? The scribe learned in the law thereupon related that when he went on board the ship, he gave a loaf of bread to a poor man, who thanked him for it, saying: As thou hast saved my life, may thy life be saved. Thereupon Akiba thought of the proverb in Ecc 11:1. Similarly the Targ.: Extend to the poor the bread for thy support; they sail in ships over the water.</note> regard this as an exhortation to charity, which although practised without expectation of reward, does not yet remain unrewarded at last. An Aram. proverb of Ben Sira’s (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Buxtorf’s <hi type="italic">Florilegium</hi>, p. 171) proceeds on this interpretation: “Scatter thy bread on the water and on the dry land; in the end of the days thou findest it again.” Knobel quotes a similar Arab. proverb from Diez' <hi type="italic">Denkwürdigkeiten von Asien</hi> (Souvenirs of Asia), II 106: “Do good; cast thy bread into the water: thou shalt be repaid some day.” See also the proverb in Goethe’s <hi type="italic">Westöst. Divan</hi>, compared by Herzfeld. Voltaire, in his <hi type="italic">Précis de l'Ecclésiaste en vers</hi>, also adopts this rendering:<hi type="italic">Repandez vos bien faits avec magnificence, Même aux moins vertueux ne les refusez pas. Ne vous informez pas de leur reconnaissance - Il est grand, il est beau de faire des ingrats</hi>. <div eID="gen12384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12385" type="x-p"/> That instead of “into the water (the sea)” of these or similar proverbs, Koheleth uses here the expression, “on the face of (על־פּני) the waters,” makes no difference: Eastern bread has for the most part the form of cakes, and is thin (especially such as is prepared hastily for guests, 'ughoth or matstsoth, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.6">Gen 18:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.3">Gen 19:3</reference>); so that when thrown into the water, it remains on the surface (like a chip of wood, Hos 10:7), and is carried away by the stream. But שׁלּח, with this reference of the proverb to beneficence, is strange; instead of it, the word השׁלך was rather to be expected; the lxx renders by ἀπόστειλον; the Syr., shadar; Jerome, <hi type="italic">mitte</hi>; Venet. πέμπε; thus by none is the pure idea of casting forth connected with שׁלּח. And the reason given does not harmonize with this reference: “for in the course of many days (berov yamin, cf. mērov yamim, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.22">Isa 24:22</reference>) wilt thou find it” (not “find it again,” which would be expressed by תּשׁוּב תּם). This indefinite designation of time, which yet definitely points to the remote future, does not thus indicate that the subject is the recompense of noble self-renunciation which is sooner or later rewarded, and often immediately, but exactly accords with the idea of commerce carried on with foreign countries, which expects to attain its object only after a long period of waiting. In the proper sense, they send their bread over the surface of the water who, as <reference osisRef="Ps.107.33">Psa 107:33</reference> expresses, “do business in great waters.” It is a figure taken from the corn trade of a seaport, an illustration of the thought: seek thy support in the way of bold, confident adventure.<note placement="foot">The Greek phrase σπείρειν πόντον, “to sow the sea” = to undertake a fruitless work, is of an altogether different character; cf. Amo 6:12.</note> <div eID="gen12385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12386" type="x-p"/> Bread in לח is the designation of the means of making a living or gain, and bread in תּמצאנּוּ the designation of the gain (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">Ecc 9:11</reference>). Hitzig’s explanation: Throw thy bread into the water = venture thy hope, is forced; and of the same character are all the attempts to understand the word of agricultural pursuits; <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by van der Palm: <hi type="italic">sementem fac muxta aquas</hi> (or: <hi type="italic">in loca irrigua</hi>); Grätz even translates: “Throw thy corn on the surface of the water,” and understands this, with the fancy of a Martial, of begetting children. Mendelssohn is right in remarking that the exhortation shows itself to be that of Koheleth-Solomon, whose ships traded to Tarshish and Ophir. Only the reference to self-sacrificing beneficence stands on a level with it as worthy of consideration. With Ginsburg, we may in this way say that a proverb as to our dealings with those who are above us, is followed by a proverb regarding those who are below us; with those others a proverb regarding judicious courageous venturing, ranks itself with a proverb regarding a rashness which is to be discountenanced; and the following proverb does not say: Give a portion, distribute of that which is thine, to seven and also to eight: for it is well done that thou gainest for thee friends with the unrighteous mammon for a time when thou thyself mayest unexpectedly be in want; but it is a prudent rule which is here placed by the side of counsel to bold adventure:
entries.f554ef5a626eab9e8db197a36ad77150dd8fa36b: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ecc 11:2</reference> “Divide the portion into seven, yea, eight (parts); for thou knowest not what evil shall happen on the earth.” With that other interpretation, עליך was to be expected instead of 'al-haarets; for an evil spreading abroad over the earth, a calamity to the land, does not yet fall on every one without exception; and why was not the רעה designated directly as personal? The impression of the words לשׁם ... תּן־, established in this general manner, is certainly this, that on the supposition of the possibility of a universal catastrophe breaking in, they advise a division of our property, so that if we are involved in it, our all may not at once be lost, but only this or that part of it, as Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.9">Gen 32:9</reference>, says. With reference to 1 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, it is most natural to suppose that one is counselled not to venture his all in one expedition, so that if this is lost in a storm, all might not at once be lost (Mendelss., Preston, Hitz., Stuart); with the same right, since 1 <hi type="italic">a</hi> is only an example, the counsel may be regarded as denoting that one must not commit all to one caravan; or, since in <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ecc 11:2</reference> לחמך is to be represented not merely as a means of obtaining gain, that one ought not to lay up all he has gathered in one place, Jdg 6:11; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.8">Jer 41:8</reference> (Nachtigal); in short, that one ought not to put all into one business, or, as we say literally, venture all on one card. חלק is either the portion which one possesses, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the measure of the possession that has fallen to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>), or חלק נתן means to make portions, to undertake a division. In the first case, the expression ל ... נתן follows the scheme of <reference osisRef="Gen.17.20">Gen 17:20</reference> : make the part into seven, yea, into eight (parts); in the second case, the scheme of <reference osisRef="Josh.18.5">Jos 18:5</reference> : make division into seven, etc. We prefer the former, because otherwise that which is to be divided remains unknown; חלק is the part now in possession: make the much or the little that thou hast into seven or yet more parts. The rising from seven to eight is as at <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">Job 5:19</reference>, and like the expression <hi type="italic">ter quaterque</hi>, etc. The same inverted order of words as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ecc 11:2</reference></hi> is found in <reference osisRef="Esth.6.3">Est 6:3</reference>; 2Ki 8:12.
entries.4b6a06d53167ea5460fcb7fc0c10b92b9dcaa356: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Ecc 11:3</reference> <div eID="gen12386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12387" type="x-p"/> With this verse there is not now a transition, εἰς ἄλλο γένος (as when one understands Ecc 11:1. of beneficence); the thoughts down to <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">Ecc 11:6</reference> move in the same track. “When the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth: and if a tree fall in the south, or in the north - the place where the tree falleth, there it lieth.” Man knows not - this is the reference of the verse backwards - what misfortune, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, hurricane, flood, scarcity, will come upon the earth; for all that is done follows fixed laws, and the binding together of cause and effect is removed beyond the influence of the will of man, and also in individual cases beyond his knowledge. The interpunction of 3 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: אם־ימּלאוּ העבים גּשׁם (not as by v. d. Hooght, Mendelss., and elsewhere העבים, but as the Venet. 1515, 21, Michael. העבים, for immediately before the tone syllable <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> is changed into <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>) appears on the first glance to be erroneous, and much rather it appears that the accentuation ought to be אם־ימלאו העבים גשם על־הארץ יריקו but on closer inspection גשׁם is rightly referred to the conditional antecedent, for “the clouds could be filled also with hail, and thus not pour down rain” (Hitz.). As in <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.10">Ecc 4:10</reference>, the fut. stands in the protasis as well as in the apodosis. If A is done, then as a consequence B will be done; the old language would prefer the words והריקו ... נמלאו (כי) אם, Ewald, §355 <hi type="italic">b</hi>: as often as A happens, so always happens B. יריקוּ carries (without needing an external object to be supplied), as internally transitive, its object is itself: if the clouds above fill themselves with rain, they make an emptying, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, they empty themselves downwards. Man cannot, if the previous condition is fixed, change the necessary consequences of it. <div eID="gen12387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12388" type="x-p"/> The second conditioning clause: <hi type="italic">si ceciderit lignum ad austraum aut ad aquilonem, in quocunque loco cociderit ibi erit</hi>. Thus rightly Jerome. It might also be said: ואם־יפול עץ אם בדרום ואם בחפין, and if a tree falls, whether it be in the south or in the north; this <hi type="italic">sive</hi> ... <hi type="italic">sive</hi> would thus be a parenthetic parallel definition. Thus regarded, the protasis as it lies before us consists in itself, as the two veim in <reference osisRef="Amos.9.3">Amo 9:3</reference>, of two correlated halves: “And if a tree falls on the south side, and (or) if it fall on the north side,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, whether it fall on the one or on the other. The <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, which more correctly belongs to יריקי, sets off in an expressive way the protasis over against the apodosis; that a new clause begins with veim yippol is unmistakeable; for the contrary, there was need for a chief disjunctive to בץ. Meqom is <hi type="italic">accus. loci</hi> for bimqom, as at <reference osisRef="Esth.4.3">Est 4:3</reference>; Est 8:17. Sham is rightly not connected with the relat. clause (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.13">Eze 6:13</reference>); the relation is the same as at Est 1:7. The fut. יהוּא is formed from הוה, whence <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.22">Ecc 2:22</reference>, as at <reference osisRef="Neh.6.6">Neh 6:6</reference>, and in the Mishna (<hi type="italic">Aboth</hi>, vi. 1;<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Baer, <hi type="italic">Abodath Jisrael</hi>, p. 290.</note><hi type="italic">Aboda zara</hi>, iii. 8) the part. הוה. As the jussive form יהי is formed from יהיה, so יהיה (יהוה) passes into יהוּ, which is here written יהוּא. Hitzig supposes that, according to the passage before us and <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference>, the word appears to have been written with א, in the sense of “to fall.” Certainly הוה has the root-signification of <hi type="italic">delabi</hi>, <hi type="italic">cadere</hi>, and derives from thence the meaning of <hi type="italic">accidere</hi>, <hi type="italic">exsistere</hi>, <hi type="italic">esse</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference>); in the Book of Job, however, הוה may have this meaning as an Arabism; in the <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>. of the author of the Book of Koheleth it certainly was no longer so used. Rather it may be said that יהוּ had to be written with an א added to distinguish it from the abbreviated tetragramm, if the א, as in אבוּא, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">Isa 28:12</reference>, and הל, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>, does not merely represent the long terminal vowel (cf. the German-Jewish דוא = thou, דיא = the, etc.).<note placement="foot">Otherwise Ewald, §192b: יהוּא, Aram. of הוּא (as בּוא) = הוא.</note> <div eID="gen12388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12389" type="x-p"/> Moreover, יהוּא, as written, approaches the Mishnic inflection of the fut. of the verb הוה; the sing. there is יהא, תּהא, אהא, and the plur. יהוּ, according to which Rashi, Aben Ezra, and Kimchi interpret יהוּא here also as plur.; Luzzatto, §670, hesitates, but in his Commentary he takes it as sing., as the context requires: there will it (the tree) be, or in accordance with the more lively meaning of the verb הוה: there will it find itself, there it continues to lie. As it is an invariable law of nature according to which the clouds discharge the masses of water that have become too heavy for them, so it is an unchangeable law of nature that the tree that has fallen before the axe or the tempest follows the direction in which it is impelled. Thus the future forms itself according to laws beyond the control of the human will, and man also has no certain knowledge of the future; wherefore he does well to be composed as to the worst, and to adopt prudent preventive measures regarding it. This is the reference of <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Ecc 11:3</reference> looking backwards. But, on the other hand, from this incalculableness of the future-this is the reference of <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Ecc 11:3</reference> looking forwards-he ought not to vie up fresh venturesome activity, much rather he ought to abstain from useless and impeding calculations and scruples.
entries.f0376a183666db4fcefd551d1c039d7015f9dded: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Ecc 11:4</reference> “He who observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.” The proverb is not to be understood literally, but in the spirit of the whole <hi type="italic">paraenesis</hi>: it is not directed against the provident observation, guided by experience, of the monitions and warnings lying in the present condition of the weather, but against that useless, because impossible, calculation of the coming state of the weather, which waits on from day to day, from week to week, till the right time for sowing and reaping has passed away. The seed-time requires rain so as to open up and moisten the ground; he who has too much hesitation observes (שׁמר) the wind whether it will bring rain (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference>), and on that account puts off the sowing of the seed till it is too late. The time of harvest requires warmth without rain (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">Pro 26:1</reference>); but the scrupulous and timid man, who can never be sure enough, looks at the clouds (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Isa 47:13</reference>), scents rainy weather, and finds now and never any security for the right weather for the gathering in of the fruits of the field. He who would accomplish and gain anything, must have confidence and courage to venture something; the conditions of success cannot be wholly reckoned upon, the future is in the hand of God, the All-Conditioning.
entries.c75879501b8267376d97a23287261733f2a22865: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference> “As thou hast no knowledge what is the way of the wind, like as the bones in the womb of her who is with child; so thou knowest not the work of God who accomplisheth all.” Luther, after Jerome, renders rightly: “As thou knowest not the way of the wind, and how the bones in the mother’s womb do grow; so,” etc. The clause, <hi type="italic">instar ossium in ventre praegnantis</hi>, is the so-called <hi type="italic">comparatio decurtata for instar ignorantiae tuae ossium</hi>, etc., like thy ignorance regarding the bones, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the growth of the bones. כּעץ,<note placement="foot">The Targ. reads בעץ, and construes: What the way of the spirit in the bones, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, how the embryo becomes animated.</note> because more closely defined by 'בּב הם, has not the art. used elsewhere after כ of comparison; an example for the regular syntax (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Riehm, under <reference osisRef="Ps.17.12">Psa 17:12</reference>) is found at Deu 32:2. That man has no power over the wind, we read at <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Ecc 8:8</reference>; the way of the wind he knows not (Joh 3:8), because he has not the wind under his control: man knows fundamentally only that which he rules. Regarding the origin and development of the embryo as a  secret which remained a mystery to the Israel. <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 209ff. For עצם, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference> and Job 10:11. Regarding meleah, pregnant (like the Lat. <hi type="italic">plena</hi>). With fine discrimination, the fut. תדע לא in the apodosis interchanges with the particip. יודע אינך in the protasis, as when we say: If thou knowest not that, as a consequence thou shalt also not know this. As a man must confess his ignorance in respect to the way of the wind, and the formation of the child in the mother’s womb; so in general the work of God the All-Working lies beyond his knowledge: he can neither penetrate it in the entireness of its connection, nor in the details of its accomplishment. The idea 'oseh kol, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference>, is intentionally unfolded in a fut. relat. clause, because here the fut. in the natural world, as well as in human history, comes principally into view. For that very reason the words את־הכּל are also used, not: (as in passages where there is a reference to the world of creation in its present condition) eth-kol-elleh, Isa 66:2. Also the growth of the child in the mother’s womb is compared to the growth of the future in the womb of the present, out of which it is born (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Pro 27:1</reference>; cf. Zep 2:2). What is established by this proof that man is not lord of the future, - viz. that in the activity of his calling he should shake off anxious concern about the future, - is once again inferred with the combination of what is said in <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Ecc 11:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ecc 11:2</reference> (according to our interpretation, here confirmed).
entries.3ad5ccd6bc290cee9550e1203a47e4ddae3d5f23: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">Ecc 11:6</reference> “In the morning sow thy seed, and towards evening withdraw not thine hand; for thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that, or whether both together shall well succeed.” The cultivation of the land is the prototype of all labour (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.15">Gen 2:15</reference>), and sowing is therefore an emblem of all activity in one’s pursuit; this general meaning for ידך ... אל־ (like <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:18</reference>; synon. with ידך ... אל־, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.6">Jos 10:6</reference>, of the older language) is to be accepted. The parallel word to babokěr is not ba'ěTrěv; for the cessation from work (Jdg 19:16; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.23">Psa 104:23</reference>) must not be excluded, but incessant labour (cf. <reference osisRef="Luke.9.62">Luk 9:62</reference>) must be continued until the evening. And as <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ecc 11:2</reference> counsels that one should not make his success depend exclusively on one enterprise, but should divide that which he has to dispose of, and at the same time make manifold trials; so here also we have the reason for restless activity of manifold labour from morning till evening: success or failure (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.5">Ecc 5:5</reference>) is in the hand of God, - man knows not which (<hi type="italic">quid</hi>, here, according to the sense, <hi type="italic">utrum</hi>) will prosper, whether (ה) this or (או) that, and whether (אמו), etc.; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding the three-membered disjunctive question, Ewald, §361; and regarding keěhhad, it is in common use in the more modern language, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, also in the last benediction of the <hi type="italic">Shemone-Esra</hi>: כאחד ... ברכנו, “bless us, our Father, us all together.” שׁניהם goes back to the two זה, understood neut. (as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:18</reference>; cf. on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.5">Ecc 6:5</reference>). The lxx rightly: καὶ ἐὰν (better: εἴτε) τὰ δύο επὶτὸ αυτὸ ἀγατηά. Luther, who translates: “and if both together it shall be better,” has been misled by Jerome. <div eID="gen12389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12390" type="x-p"/> The proverb now following shows its connection with the preceding by the copula <hi type="italic">vav</hi>. “The tendency of the advice in <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Ecc 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ecc 11:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">Ecc 11:6</reference>, to secure guarantees for life, is justified in <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7">Ecc 11:7</reference> : life is beautiful, and worthy of being cared for.” Thus Hitzig; but the connection is simpler. It is in the spirit of the whole book that, along with the call to earnest activity, there should be the call to the pleasant enjoyment of life: he who faithfully labours has a right to enjoy his life; and this joy of life, based on fidelity to one’s calling, and consecrated by the fear of God, is the most real and the highest enjoyment here below. In this sense the <hi type="italic">fruere vita</hi> here connects itself with the labora:
entries.4906ac4b56ed51dbb2b13be39a56f7815f9fec92: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7-Eccl.11.8">Ecc 11:7-8</reference> “And sweet is the light, and pleasant it is for the eyes to see the sun; for if a man live through many years, he ought to rejoice in them all, and remember the days of darkness; that there will be many of them. All that cometh is vain.” Dale translates the copula vav introducing <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7">Ecc 11:7</reference> by “yes,” and Bullock by “truly,” both thus giving to it a false colouring. “Light,” Zöckler remarks, stands here for “life.” But it means only what the word denotes, viz., the light of life in this world (Ps. 56:14; <reference osisRef="Job.33.30">Job 33:30</reference>), to which the sun, as the source of it, is related, as מאור is to אור. Cf. Eurip. <hi type="italic">Hippol</hi>., ὧ λαμπρὸς αἰθὴρ κ.τ.λ, and <hi type="italic">Iphigen. in Aulis</hi>, 1218-19, μὴ μ ̓ ἀπολέσης κ.τ.λ: “Destroy not my youth; to see the light is sweet,” etc. The ל in לע has the short vowel <hi type="italic">Pattach</hi>, here and at <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>, after the Masora.<note placement="foot">Cf. on the contrary, at <reference osisRef="Gen.3.6">Gen 3:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.10.26">Pro 10:26</reference>, where it has the <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>; cf. also <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 53 <hi type="italic">b</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12391" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">ki</hi> beginning <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.8">Ecc 11:8</reference> is translated by Knobel, Hitz., Ewald, and others by “<hi type="italic">ja</hi>” (yes); by Heiligstedt, as if a negative preceded by <hi type="italic">immo</hi>; but as the <hi type="italic">vav</hi> of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7">Ecc 11:7</reference></hi> is copulative “and,” so here the <hi type="italic">ki</hi> is causal “for.” If it had been said: man must enjoy himself as long as he lives, for the light is sweet, etc., then the joy would have its reason in the opportunity given for it. Instead of this, the occasion given for joy has its reason in this, that a man ought to rejoice, viz., according to God’s arrangement and ordinance: the light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun; for it ought thus to be, that a man, however long he may live, should continue to enjoy his fair life, especially in view of the night which awaits him. <hi type="italic">Ki im</hi> are not here, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ecc 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">Ecc 8:15</reference>, where a negative precedes, to be taken together; but <hi type="italic">ki</hi> assigns the reason, and im begins a hypothetical protasis, as at <reference osisRef="Exod.8.17">Exo 8:17</reference>, and frequently. <hi type="italic">Im</hi>, with the conclusion following, presents something impossible, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Psa 50:12</reference>, <hi type="italic">si esurirem</hi>, or also the extreme of that which is possible as actual, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference>, <hi type="italic">si peccata vestra sint instar coccini</hi>. In the latter case, the clause with the concessive particle may be changed into a sentence with a concessive conjunctive, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference> : “for though thy people, O Israel, be as numerous as the sand of the sea;” and here: “though a man may live ever so many years.” The second <hi type="italic">ki</hi> after ויז is the explicat. <hi type="italic">quod</hi>, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Ecc 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4">Ecc 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ecc 8:17</reference>, etc.: he must remember the days of darkness, that there shall be many of them, and, at all events, not fewer than the many years available for the happy enjoyment of life. In this connection kol-shebba' denotes all that will come after this life. If Hitz. remarks that the sentence: “All that is future is vanity,” is a false thought, this may now also be said of his own sentence extracted from the words: “All that is, is transitory.” For all that is done, in time may pass away; but it is not actually transitory (הבל). But the sentence also respects not all that is future, but all that comes after this life, which must appear as vain (hěvel) to him for whom, as for Koheleth, the future is not less veiled in the dark night of Hades, as it was for Horace, i. 4. 16 s.:<hi type="italic">“Jam te premet nox fabulaeque Manes Et domus exilis Plutonia.”</hi> <div eID="gen12391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12392" type="x-p"/> Also, for Koheleth as for Horace, iv. 7. 16, man at last becomes <hi type="italic">pulvis et umbra</hi>, and that which thus awaits him is hevel. Tyler is right, that “the shadowy and unsubstantial condition of the dead and the darkness of Sheol” is thus referred to. הבּא signifies not that which is <hi type="italic">nascens</hi>, but <hi type="italic">futurum</hi>, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 27 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, “from the present ולהבא and for the future” (for which, elsewhere, the expression לעתיד לבא is used). The Venet. construes falsely: All (the days) in which vanity will overtake (him); and Luther, referring בא as the 3rd pers. to the past, follows the misleading of Jerome. Rightly the lxx and Theod.: πᾶν τὸ ἐρξηόμενον.
entries.50312e88ca6e69088bbbd596d2e894f53600c915: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ecc 11:9</reference> “Rejoice, young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know, that for all this God will bring thee to judgment.” The parallel בּימי shows that the <hi type="italic">beth</hi> in בּילד (with ד aspirated) does not introduce the reason of the joy, but the time suitable for it. Instead of veyithav libbecha, “let thy heart be of good cheer,” as the expression might also be, the words are vithivecha libbecha, “make thy heart of good cheer to thee,” - so, viz., that from this centre brightness may irradiate thy countenance (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.13">Pro 15:13</reference>) and thy whole personality, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 249.
