Vehhuroth, the period of youth, is here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Ecc 12:1</reference> = Num 11:28, vehhurim, as the only once occurring ne'uroth, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.30">Jer 32:30</reference>, is = the elsewhere generally used ne'urim; the form in ôth is the more modern (cf. keluloth, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer 2:2</reference>). “Ways of the heart” are thus ways into which the impulse of the heart leads, and which satisfy the heart. מר עין, at <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.9">Ecc 6:9</reference>, designates the pleasure felt in the presence of the object before one; here, a sight which draws and fastens the eyes upon it. The Chethı̂b has the plur. מראי, which is known to the language (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.15">Dan 1:15</reference>; Sol 2:14), and which would here designate the multitude of the objects which delight the eyes, which is not unsuitable; the <hi type="italic">Pih</hi>. הלּך denotes also elsewhere, frequently, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.131.1">Psa 131:1</reference>, walking, in an ethical sense; Hitz., Zöckl., and others interpret the first ב as specifying the sphere, and the second as specifying the norm (“according to the sight of thine eyes”); but they both introduce that wherein he ought to act freely and joyfully: in the ways of thy heart, into which it draws thee; and in the sight of thine eyes, towards which they direct themselves with interest. The lxx B. renders, “and not after the sight of thine eyes.” This “not” (μή), which is wanting in A.C., is an interpolation, in view of the warning, Num 15:39, against following the impulse of the heart and of the eyes; the Targ. also therefore has: “be prudent with reference to the sight of thine eyes.” But this moralizing of the text is superfluous, since the call to the youthful enjoyment of life is accompanied with the <hi type="italic">nota bene</hi>: but know that God will bring thee to an account for all this; and thus it excludes sinful sensual desire. In the midst of an address, where a yet closer definition follows, בּמש is thus punctuated, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">Ecc 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.3">Job 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">Psa 143:3</reference>; here, in the conclusion of the sentence, it is במש. Hitzig supposes that there is denoted by it, that the sins of youth are punished by chronic disease and abandonment in old age; Knobel and others understand by the judgment, the self-punishment of sins by all manner of evil consequences, which the O.T. looks upon as divinely inflicted penalties. But in view of the facts of experience, that God’s righteous requital is in this life too frequently escaped, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ecc 8:14</reference>, the author, here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ecc 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">Ecc 12:14</reference>, postulates a final judgment, which removes the contradiction of this present time, and which must thus be in the future; he has no clear idea of the time and manner of this final judgment, but his faith in God places the certainty of it beyond all doubt. The call to rejoice is now completed by the call to avoid all that occasions inward and outward sorrow.
entries.a7c1528387b45b3325c4ef54f392dd61218097e9: <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.10">Ecc 11:10</reference> “And remove sorrow from thy heart, and banish evil from thy flesh: for youth and age, not yet grown to grey hairs, are vain.” Jerome translates: <hi type="italic">aufer iram a corde tuo</hi>, and remarks in his <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>.: <hi type="italic">in ira omnes perturbationes animi comprehendit</hi>; but כּעס (R. כס, <hi type="italic">contundere</hi>, <hi type="italic">confringere</hi>) does not signify anger, but includes both anger and sorrow, and thus corresponds to the specific ideas, “sadness, moroseness, fretfulness.” The clause following, Jerome translates:<hi type="italic">et amove malitiam a carne tua</hi>, with the remark: <hi type="italic">in carnis malitia universas significat corporis voluptates</hi>; but רעה is not taken in an ethical, but in a physical sense: כעס is that which brings sorrow to the heart; and רעה, that which brings evil to the flesh (בשׂר, opp. לב, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Ecc 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.30">Pro 14:30</reference>). More correctly than the Vulgate, Luther renders: “banish sorrow from thy heart, and put evil from thy body.” He ought to free himself from that which is injurious to the inner and the outer man, and hurtfully affects it; for youth, destined for and disposed to joy, is hevel, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, transitory, and only too soon passes away. Almost all modern interpreters (excepting the Jewish), in view of <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>, gives to שׁחרוּת the meaning of “the dawn of the morning;” but the connection with ילדוּת would then be tautological; the Mishn.-Midrash <hi type="italic">usus loq.</hi>, in conformity with which the Targ. translates, “days of black hair,” proves that the word does not go back to שׁחר, morning dawn, morning-red, but immediately to שׁחור, black, and as the contrast of שׂיבה (non-bibl. שׂיבוּת, סיב, סב), <hi type="italic">canities</hi>, denotes the time of black hair, and thus, in the compass of its conception, goes beyond ילדות, since it comprehends both the period of youth and of manhood, and thus the whole period during which the strength of life remains unbroken.<note placement="foot">The Mishna, <hi type="italic">Nedarim</hi> iii. 8, jurist. determines that שׁחורי הראשׁ denotes men, with the exclusion of women (whose hair is covered) and children. It is disputed (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Abodath Jisrael</hi>, p. 279) whether תּשׁחרת, <hi type="italic">Aboth</hi> iii. 16, <hi type="italic">Derech erez</hi> c. II., <hi type="italic">Midrash</hi> under <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">Lam 2:11</reference>, is = שׁחרוּת, but without right; ben-tishhorěth is used for a grown-up son in full manly strength.</note>  <chapter eID="Eccl.11"/> <div eID="gen12392" type="x-p"/>

entries.c8680018701b05adc2b5c010b14ab16337b2fec3:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="11" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:554" />
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 CAst thy bread <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> upon <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> face of the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> upon the waters <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> having discovered diverse vanities, and amongst o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers the vanity of heaping up Riches, he now teacheth us that it is our Interest as well as Duty, not so much to lay them up, as to lay them out in pious and charitable uses; and having taught us the true and best use of worldly things, for our present comfort and benefit, which is to enjoy them with a chearful and contented Mind, he now directs us to the best improvement of them, for our future and greater advantage; and having acquainted us with our duty towards our Superiours, he now directs us in our carriage towards our Inferiours, and especially to such of them as are poor. The sense of these words is either 1. <ns0:hi>Cast thy seed</ns0:hi> (which is here called <ns0:hi>Bread,</ns0:hi> as it is also <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 28. 5. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28. 28. and elsewhere) <ns0:hi>be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />side</ns0:hi> (for so the Hebrew particle, <ns0:hi>al,</ns0:hi> is oft used) <ns0:hi>the waters, i. e.</ns0:hi> ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther by the Rivers side, or in moist and waterish grounds, which usually are very fruitful. Or 2. <ns0:hi>Cast</ns0:hi> (freely and liberally bestow) <ns0:hi>thy bread (i. e.</ns0:hi> thy Money or Provisions, which are oft signified by the name of <ns0:hi>bread.</ns0:hi> By saying <ns0:hi>thy bread,</ns0:hi> he cautions us that we give away only that which is our own, and not that which is anothers; as they do who give either what they get from others by fraud or power, or what they owe to others, and are unable to pay, and so exercise Charity to the hindrance of Justice, or of the payment of their just debts,) <ns0:hi>upon the waters, i. e.</ns0:hi> upon those poor Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, upon whom, by reason of their unthankfulness or inability to make any returns to thee, it may seem to be as utterly lost as the seed which a man casts into the Sea or River. This sense a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grees much better, 1. With the words; for he doth not barely mention <ns0:hi>the waters,</ns0:hi> (for then the particle, <ns0:hi>al,</ns0:hi> might have been translated <ns0:hi>beside</ns0:hi>) but <ns0:hi>the face, i. e.</ns0:hi> the surface or top, <ns0:hi>of the waters,</ns0:hi> in which, and such like cases, <ns0:hi>al,</ns0:hi> constantly signifies <ns0:hi>upon.</ns0:hi> 2. With the design and scope of the place, which is to persuade men to be liberal and charitable, notwithstanding the discouragements which they meet with in so doing, of which see the next clause, and the next verse.</ns0:note>; for thou shalt find it <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It shall not be lost, as covetous men, or thine own corrupt heart, may suggest, but it shall certainly be restored unto thee, either by God or by Men, and that with great Honour and Advantage. This is added to prevent an objection, and to quicken us to the duty enjoined.</ns0:note> after <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 15. 10. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 19. 17. Mat. 10. 42.</ns0:note> many days <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not immediately, but in due time, and when you least expect it. So you must be content to wait for it with Patience, as the Husbandman doth for the fruits of the Earth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">P<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 112. 9. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 6. 30.</ns0:note> Give a portion <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">A part of thy Estate or Provisions. He alludes to the ancient custom, whereby the Master of the Feast did distribute several parts to each Guest, and withal sent portions to the poor: of which custom see 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6. 19. <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 8. 10, 12. <ns0:hi>Est.</ns0:hi> 9. 22.</ns0:note> to seven, and also to eight <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To as ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny as thou art able; a certain number for an uncertain, as <ns0:hi>Mic.</ns0:hi> 5. 5. and oft elsewhere.</ns0:note>; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Great calamities may come, whereby thou maist be brought to poverty, & so both utterly lose that blessed oppor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tunity of doing good, which now thou hast in thine hands, whereby thou maist gain unspeakable Honour, and Comfort, and Advantage to thy self, and moreover need the Charity of others, which thou maist comfortably expect, either from Men, or at least from the powerful Providence of God, disposing the hearts of men to pity and help thee, if thou hast been kind and merciful to others, as on the contrary they can expect no Mercy from God or Men, who have shewed no Mercy to others. Thus he not only answers but retorts the Argument by which the covetous man excuseth his un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />charitableness, because he must lay up against a rainy day.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 If the clouds be full of rain, they empty <ns0:hi>them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves</ns0:hi> upon the earth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Learn, O man, the practice of liberality from the very lifeless Creatures, from the Clouds; which when they are filled with wa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, do not hoard it up, or keep it to themselves, but plentifully pour it forth for the refreshment both of the fruitful field and of the barren wilderness.</ns0:note>: and if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north; in the place where the tree falleth there it shall be <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">These words contain either 1. An Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument to persuade Men to Charity, because they must shortly fall or die, and then all opportunity of being charitable will be lost, and they must expect certainly and eternally to reap whatso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever they have sown, whether it hath been Mercy or Unmerciful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness. Or rather 2. An Answer to a common Objection against it, because we are not certain whether the person who desires our Charity doth really need it, or be worthy of it. To this he an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swers, As a Tree when it falls, either by the violence of the wind, or being cut down by its owners order, it is not considerable whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther it falls Southward or Northward, for there it lies ready for the Masters use; so thy Charity, though it may possibly be misapplied by thee, or abused by the Receiver, yet being conscientiously gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven by thee, it shall assuredly return to thee, and thou shalt reap the fruit of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 He that observeth the wind, shall not sow, and he that regardeth the clouds, shall not reap <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He who neglects or delays the necessary works of sowing and reaping, because the weather is not exactly suitable to his desires, may possibly lose his Harvest. Whereby he intimates what is easi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly understood out of the foregoing verses, that Men will never do good here, which is expressed by <ns0:hi>sowing, Psal.</ns0:hi> 112. 9. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. and consequently not receive good hereafter, which is called <ns0:hi>reap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing,</ns0:hi> Gal. 6. 7, 8. if they be discouraged and hindred from it by every doubt or difficulty, such as covetous worldlings object to themselves, that others either do not want their Charity, or will abuse it, that they may possibly need it hereafter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 As thou knowest not what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the way <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>of the wind,</ns0:hi> Joh. 3. 8.</ns0:note> of the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Of the Spirit or Soul of Man, how it first comes into the Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy of the child in the Womb, whether from God by Creation, or from the Parents by Propagation; nor how it is united with, and so fixed in the Body that it cannot get out of it when it would; nor how and whether it goes out of the Body; all which things are great mysteries. Others translate it, <ns0:hi>of the wind, whence it cometh, and whither it goeth,</ns0:hi> as is observed <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 3. 8. or how violently it will blow, or how long it will last. But the former Translation seems to agree better with the following clause.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>nor</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 139. 14, 15.</ns0:note> how the bones <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The whole Body, which is elsewhere signified by the Bones, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34. 20. & 35. 10. because they are a principal part, and the very foundation and support of the Body.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>do grow</ns0:hi> in the womb <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">How it comes to pass that one and the same small quantity of seed should diversifie itself into skin, and flesh, and sinews, and veins, and bones, and intrals, or how it receiveth nourishment and growth.</ns0:note> of her that is with child; even so thou knowest not the works of God <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">What God is doing and will do with thee or others, the Counsels and Methods of Gods Providence in the future time of thy Life, what evil God will send upon the Earth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. or what weather he will send, of which <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. how long or how little a while God will continue thy Life or Estate, and how soon God will call thee to an account. These and many other future events thou canst not foresee, and therefore thy Wisdom and Duty is to cast off all distracting cares, and distrustful fears about them, and chearfully to commit thy self, and all thy affairs, into the Hand of God in well-doing.</ns0:note> who maketh all.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 In the morning <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Early and late, in all seasons and occasions, do it speedily and continually, be not weary of it.</ns0:note> sow thy seed <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Do all good works, and e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />specially that of Alms-giving, as <ns0:hi>sowing</ns0:hi> is understood, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6. 7.</ns0:note>, and in the e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vening <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Early and late, in all seasons and occasions, do it speedily and continually, be not weary of it.</ns0:note> with-hold not thine hand <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">From working or giving.</ns0:note>: for thou know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est not whether <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> shall be right.</ns0:note> shall prosper <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which shall prosper most, as the next clause explains it; the positive Degree being put for the comparative, or the Superlative, which is not unusual in the Hebrew Text. Which shall best answer thine end, or do most good to others, or which shall tend most to the comfort of thy great and last account: for thy Morning-Alms may possibly be given to an unworthy person, or to one who did not need it, and will abuse it, and thy Evening-Alms may fall upon a person of emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent worth, yea, upon an Angel in humane shape, which is re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membred as a motive to Hospitality, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13. 2. or upon one in extream necessity, who might possibly have perished both in Soul and Body, if thou hadst not comforted and relieved him: Or, one time thou maist give with more sincere Intention, and with more tender compassion than another time, and so one will be more right and more acceptable to God than the other</ns0:note>, either this or that, or whether they both <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> alike good <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Equal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly successful to the receiver, or to the giver.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Truly the light <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> sweet, and a pleasant <ns0:hi>thing it is</ns0:hi> for the eyes to behold the sun <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">It cannot be denied that this present Life (which is called <ns0:hi>light, Iob</ns0:hi> 3. 20. & 33. 30. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 56. 13. and which is expressed Synec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dochically, by <ns0:hi>seeing the Sun, Eccl.</ns0:hi> 6. 5. & 7. 11.) is in itself a great blessing, and very desirable; but it is not perpetual nor sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tisfactory; which is here implied and expressed in the nex<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 But if a man live many years <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which is a priviledge granted but to few persons compara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tively.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> rejoice in them all <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And suppose he enjoy all the comforts, and escape all the imbitterments of humane Life, all his days: which also is a great rarity.</ns0:note>; yet let him remember <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">It is his Duty and Interest seriously to consider.</ns0:note> the days of dark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Of death, or of the state of the dead, which is oft expressed by <ns0:hi>dark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 10. 21. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 88. 12. &c. and here is opposed to the foregoing <ns0:hi>Light.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, for they shall be many <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Far more than the days of this short Life, especially if to the time of lying in the Grave be added that greater and utter darkness which is reserved for impenitent sinners, and which is everlasting, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 22. 13. & 25. 30. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2. 17. <ns0:hi>Iud. v.</ns0:hi> 13. And this is added for the caution of mankind, that they may not rejoice excessively in, nor content themselves with the happiness of the present Life, but may seek for somthing more du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable, and more satisfactory.</ns0:note>. All that cometh <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">All things which befall any man belonging only to this Life, whether they be comfortable or vexa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tious, they are but vain and inconsiderable, because they are short and transitory.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vanity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:555" />9 Rejoice <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This verse is to be understood either 1. As a serious Advice to this purpose, seeing Life is short and transitory, improve it to the best advantage, take comfort in it whilest you may, only do it with moderation, and the fear of God. Or rather 2. As an Iro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nical concession, such as are usual both in Scripture, as 1 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 18. 27. & 22. 15. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 28. 3, 4. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 26. 45. and in other Authors. For this agrees much better with the context, and with the Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressions here used. And so the sense is, I foresee what evil use some men will make of what I have now said; Things being thus, <ns0:hi>Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die,</ns0:hi> as they also reasoned, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15. 32.</ns0:note>, O young man <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He speaks to young Men particularly, because they have both the greatest ability, and the strongest Inclinations to pursue sensual pleasures, and are most impatient either of Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />straint or Admonition.</ns0:note>, in thy youth, and let thy heart chear thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Indulge thy frolick and jolly humour, and take thy fill of delights.</ns0:note> in the days of thy youth; and walk in the way of thy heart, and in the sight of thine eyes <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Whatsoever thine Eye or Heart lusteth after, deny it not to them; as this Phrase is taken, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 15. 39. nor is it ever used in a good sense. Compare <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 7. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 81. 12. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 18. 12. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2. 14. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2. 16.</ns0:note>: but know thou <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">But in the midst of thy feastings and jollity it will become thee, if thou art a reasonable Creature, to consider thy reckoning, and whether thou dost not purchase thy Gold too dear.</ns0:note>, that for all these <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For all thy <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ollies and sinful Lusts, which thou sleightest as tricks of youth.</ns0:note> God will bring thee into judgment <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Will force thee to appear before his Judgment-seat, to give a serious account of all thy youthful and exorbitant courses, and to receive that sentence which thy own Conscience will then say thou dost justly deserve. And if thou likest thy sensuality upon these terms, much good may it do thee. I do not envy thee, nor desire to par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />take of thy delicates.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Therefore remove <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> anger.</ns0:note> sorrow <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Sensual and disorderly Lusts, which he elegantly and emphatically calls <ns0:hi>sorrow,</ns0:hi> with respect to the foregoing words, to intimate, that although such practices do at present gratifie and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />light mens Senses and vain Minds, yet they will shortly and certainly bring a man to intollerable and eternal sorrows, which it is thy Wisdom to prevent.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, as it is rendred in the margent, and by divers others, <ns0:hi>anger;</ns0:hi> a passion to which men are most prone in the heat of youth Whereby he may understand either anger a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst him for this sharp admonition; or rather against God, who hath laid such severe restraints upon them, and threatens such pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishments to them for following their own natural Inclinations. So the sense is, do not quarrel with thy Judge, but submit and make thy Peace with him by declaring War against all thy Sins.</ns0:note> from thy heart, and put away evil <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">All evil Concupiscences or Lusts, which though now they seem good to thee, will another day appear to be very evil and bitter things.</ns0:note> from thy flesh <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">From thy bodily members. Which he mentions not exclusive<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, as if he would allow them their spiritual evils, but emphatical<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, because young men to whom he is here speaking, are most given to fleshly or bodily Lusts.</ns0:note>; for childhood and youth <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> vanity <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Most vain, either 1. In their temper and dispositions. Young men are frothy, and foolish, and inconsiderate, whereby they run into manifold dangers, and therefore they shall do well to hearken to the Counsels of those who by their greater Wisdom and Experience, are more capable Judges of these matters. Or 2. In their condition. The time of Youth is vanishing and transitory, and Old-age and Death will speedily come, against which every man in his wits will take care to lay in solid provisions and comforts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
